<reason>Both sides built coherent cases, but A more consistently converted rebuttal pressure into damage. A's core move — that "intake" at French food banks is not proof of consumption, and that a mandate only formalizes donation on the "easy" nights that would happen anyway while adding pure compliance cost on the "hard" nights that actually bind — was never fully dismantled. B's asymmetry framing ("certainty beats speculation") is a strong abstract structure, but it assumes the mandate changes marginal behavior, and A's closing directly attacks that assumption ("those are the nights donation already paid... the statute taxes every night for them") without B supplying a clear rebuttal beyond restating the asymmetry. B did land some real points — Good Samaritan liability protections effectively neutralized A's original risk/liability worry, and the "less ordering = less upstream waste" reframe was clever — but A's late answers mostly held the line by reframing rather than conceding, and B never revisited the liability concession to press the advantage. B's opening was also clipped for exceeding the word limit, a real execution cost per the grading rules, losing its closing weighing sentence. Overall A read as tighter, more skeptical of its opponent's central evidentiary claim, and closed with a cleaner, more falsifiable framing of what the mandate actually guarantees (labor) versus what it merely pictures (a rescued meal).</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's repeated insistence that French food-bank "intake" is a warehouse statistic, not proof of consumption — paired with the closing move that the mandate changes nothing on the nights donation was already easy and adds nothing but paperwork on the nights it's hard — was the most decisive exchange, and B's asymmetry reply never fully closed that gap.</best_rebuttal>
